Volume 08 · Chapter 10

Private equity, venture capital and entrepreneurship

Undergraduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v08-c09

By the endAnalyze illiquid ownership structures and financing incentives.

Capability and prerequisites

You can trace a private investment from its operating assets through creditors, preferred shareholders, common owners and fund investors. Begin with acquisition economics and control, the firm-to-equity cash bridge, financing incentives and contingent investment decisions. You should already distinguish an enterprise price from an equity price and an investment's value from its financing requirement. This chapter teaches the additional share-count, distribution and fund-return methods locally.

A buyout sponsor advertises a high equity return; a founder celebrates a higher post-money valuation; a fund manager reports an attractive internal rate of return. None of those numbers identifies who paid, what they own, when they can receive cash or which downside obligations remain. We will reconstruct those answers before judging performance.

Every company, fund, financing offer, tax convention and number below is an original fictional teaching input. Money is in thousands of currency units, kCU; venture share counts are in thousands of shares, so kCU divided by those counts gives CU per share. Annual dates 0, 1, 2 and 3 are exactly one year apart. These are relative case dates, not observed market data. Contract rights are stipulated and enforceable within each case; their features are not asserted to be universal legal or tax rules.

1. Follow ownership through three layers

A leveraged buyout, or LBO, acquires a business using sponsor equity and acquisition debt, with future business cash intended to service that debt. Venture capital finances young businesses whose investment opportunities and financing needs can change sharply as information arrives. Both belong to the wider study of private ownership; a buyout forecast of established cash generation is not interchangeable with a venture forecast of uncertain milestones. Kaplan and Strömberg's historical account introduces these institutional distinctions and the separation between a management firm, its funds and their portfolio companies.

At the company layer, customers provide operating receipts and suppliers, workers, the tax authority and capital investment consume cash. Company debt and equity receive the remainder according to their rights. At the fund layer, investors contribute capital to buy those company claims; the fund pays expenses and distributes proceeds. At the manager layer, the general partner or manager receives stipulated fees and performance compensation. A manager's fee revenue is not its net profit: salaries, operating expenses and taxes may still be payable.

Limited partners, or LPs, supply the fund capital in our examples. The general partner, or GP, manages investment and distribution decisions under the agreed contract. A commitment is an obligation to supply capital when validly called; it is not necessarily cash already invested. Holding cash for future calls has an opportunity cost, even if a reported fund IRR starts only when cash is called. A restriction on withdrawal, a thin secondary market or a contractual transfer restriction makes an interest illiquid; neither a recent valuation nor an accounting mark guarantees an immediately executable sale.

2. Build the buyout from uses, cash and debt

A sources-and-uses table is a closing-date budget. It cannot establish that the acquisition is attractive, but it can expose missing money. If the seller owns operating assets priced at enterprise value EV0, transferable excess cash C and debt Dold to be retired at that amount, the seller's equity proceeds are EV0+C−Dold. Acquiring the equity and retiring debt therefore uses EV0+C before transaction fees. Sources can include new debt, sponsor equity and the acquired excess cash if legally available at closing. Required operating cash is not excess cash.

Let Dt−1 be opening acquisition debt, i its annual cash interest rate, Bt EBITDA, At depreciation, Kt capital expenditure and ΔNt the increase in operating working capital. Within a case with current usable interest deductions, positive taxable profit and tax rate τ,

It = iDt−1; taxt = τ(Bt−At−It);
cash before principal = Bt−taxt−It−Kt−ΔNt
= FCFFt−(1−τ)It, where FCFFt = (Bt−At)(1−τ)+At−Kt−ΔNt.

Depreciation affects tax but is not a current cash payment. Principal repayment is a financing use, not a second deduction from taxable operating income. A cash sweep directs available cash to debt reduction. If mandatory principal exceeds available cash, report a funding gap; do not make cash negative and continue as though a lender or sponsor had agreed to finance it. Interest must use the specified timing. Here debt repaid at year-end reduces next year's interest.

Worked example 1 — Mistral's financed acquisition

At date 0, Mistral's operating enterprise price is 360, or 6 times entry EBITDA of 60. The target has excess cash 20 and old debt 80, retired at par. Necessary operating cash is already included in the operating working capital retained by the business and is excluded from the 20. Seller equity proceeds are 360+20−80 = 300. The deal fee is 10 and a fee to a third-party financing adviser is 4; neither fee receives a tax deduction in this case. The acquired company retains its stipulated depreciation basis: there is no acquisition tax step-up.

These terms are assumptions of a conditional forecast, not evidence that real lenders would offer them at this business risk. 3. Explain the gain without calling leverage free value

For a simple no-dividend buyout, write EV0 = m0B0 and EVT = mTBT. Entry sponsor capital is EV0−D0+entry fees after the acquired excess cash is used. If no later sponsor contributions occur, the final equity receipt minus initial sponsor capital is

Equity cash gain = m0(BT−B0) + (mT−m0)BT
+ (D0−DT) − entry fees − exit fees.

This ordering first changes operating earnings at the entry multiple, then changes the multiple on exit earnings. Reversing the order reallocates the interaction term; neither is a uniquely causal attribution. For Mistral the components are 72 + 0 + 61.76184 − 14 − 8 = 111.76184, equal to 275.76184−164. A larger purchase price increases required sponsor capital when debt is fixed; it is not erased by the debt schedule.

Debt paydown is funded by cash that could otherwise have remained with the company or been distributed to owners. Count that cash once. Leverage concentrates the residual payoff and may raise a successful path's percentage equity return while increasing losses and funding exposure on other paths. Under the conditions of financing irrelevance, reshuffling fairly priced claims creates no operating value. Tax effects, fees, incentives and distress can change value, but require their own cash and behavioral assumptions. Mistral's debt-service receipts discounted at its contractual 8% equal the 210 advance along this repayment path; this accounting identity does not establish an appropriate expected return on risky debt.

A funding downside makes the distinction concrete. If first-year EBITDA is 50 rather than 64, keeping that year's other inputs fixed, tax is 0.25(50−12−16.8) = 5.3. Cash before principal is 8.9, leaving a 6.1 shortfall against mandatory principal of 15. The original financing plan fails. A later exercise explicitly authorizes a sponsor contribution at date 1 and recalculates subsequent debt and returns. An unsupported assumption that the company can refinance merely moves the missing-money problem to a new lender.

An exit can be a sale to an operating buyer, another financial sponsor or a sale of shares following an IPO. The contractual process and the cash realization date matter. A retained public stake remains exposed to price changes and sale restrictions; its quoted value is not yet sale cash. A refinancing can fund a distribution only if available cash and new obligations are both recorded. Exit multiples should be consistent with the business's growth, risk, cash conversion and reinvestment, using the comparability discipline; an unchanged multiple is a scenario, not a guarantee.

4. Price the issued shares and state the denominator

A primary financing issues new company shares for new cash paid to the company. A secondary purchase transfers existing shares and pays the selling holder; it does not supply operating cash unless another transaction does so. In a priced primary round, pre-money V is the contractual valuation used to price the specified pre-round capitalization, investment J is new cash, and headline post-money is V+J. If the pricing denominator is S shares, the issue price is p = V/S and new shares equal J/p. With the same conversion basis for all counted shares, new investors' fully diluted fraction is J/(V+J).

Fully diluted means the contract's chosen count assuming specified convertible securities and awards become common shares. It must say which awards and reserves enter, at what conversion or exercise terms, and whether a new pool is created before or after pricing. It is a capitalization convention, not necessarily the count of currently issued voting shares. A reserved but ungranted option pool is not a current owner entitled to a cash distribution.

For an original share count Sold, a newly created pre-round pool P, investment-to-pre-money ratio a = J/V and target pool fraction h of the post-round fully diluted total, new investor shares are a(Sold+P), so

P = h(1+a)(Sold+P), hence
P = h(1+a)Sold/[1−h(1+a)], provided h(1+a) < 1.

The feasibility restriction leaves a positive fraction for the original owners. Creating the pool after pricing instead changes who bears its dilution. The denominator must be agreed before interpreting a percentage.

Worked example 2 — Saffron's two financing rounds

Before date-0 Series A, founders hold 6,000 thousand common shares and an existing employee team holds 2,000 thousand issued, vested common shares. There are no other claims. A invests 4,000 at pre-money 16,000, including a new pre-round reserve P that must equal 10% of the post-A fully diluted total. With a = 1/4, P = (1/8)(8,000+P), so P = 8,000/7 thousand shares. The price is 16,000/(8,000+8,000/7) = 1.75 CU; A receives 16,000/7 thousand shares. The post-A total is 80,000/7 thousand.

At date 1, Series B invests 6,000 at pre-money 24,000, with no further pool increase, anti-dilution adjustment, secondary sale or transaction fee. The price is 24,000/(80,000/7) = 2.10 CU; B receives 20,000/7 thousand shares, bringing the total to 100,000/7 thousand.

Founders6,00052.5%6,00042%
Existing team2,00017.5%2,00014%
New award pool8,000/710%8,000/78%
Series A, as converted16,000/720%16,000/716%

Without the pre-A pool, founders would have held 60% after A; with it they hold 52.5%. At B, every earlier fully diluted fraction is multiplied by 0.8. This ownership dilution does not by itself establish a wealth loss: the business receives new financing and may obtain useful labor or growth opportunities. A down round issues more shares for the same cash; the effect also depends on any actual contractual conversion adjustments. None applies here.

The headline post-money amounts are 20,000 and 30,000. They price newly issued preferred securities using an as-converted denominator. They do not establish that the founders' common claim is worth 42% of 30,000. Its rights differ. All 4,000 and 6,000 are primary cash inflows when raised; they are not assumed to remain idle until exit or added again to an exit cash pot.

5. Allocate exit cash jointly across preferred classes

A liquidation preference gives a specified priority payment from the equity cash available at a stipulated event. It is not a guarantee backed by money outside that cash pot. A 1× nonparticipating convertible preferred claim can either keep its preference up to the original investment or convert to common on the specified basis and share the common residual. It does not take both. A participating claim instead takes its preference and then a specified fraction of the residual; a cap can limit that combined payment while leaving an alternative conversion right. Always read the event, seniority, accrued dividends, cap and conversion rules.

For a single preferred class with preference P, as-converted fraction s and total equity exit cash X ≥ 0, with no other claims or dividends, nonparticipating proceeds are max[min(P, X), sX]. Uncapped participating proceeds are min(P, X)+s max(X−P, 0). If combined participating proceeds are capped at kP, k ≥ 1, and optional conversion to common remains available, proceeds are max{sX, min[kP, min(P, X)+s max(X−P, 0)]}. In each formula common receives X minus the preferred payment. These are stated contracts, not definitions that override different documents.

With several preferred classes, the residual and its sharing denominator depend on which other classes convert. Applying max(preference, final fully diluted fraction × total cash) independently to each class can violate its actual rights. The MIT contractual-payoff lecture motivates the distinction between preferred and common payoffs and why a headline round valuation cannot simply be assigned to every share. The following joint calculation is original.

Worked example 3 — Two preferences, one exit pot

Use Saffron's post-B capitalization. Before exit, every share reserved in the pool has actually been granted, vested and exercised at zero exercise price into common; there is no exercise cash, unissued pool or forfeiture at exit. This simplifying award contract is not a tax or compensation recommendation. Common holders together have 64% of the all-converted count, A 16% and B 20%.

A has a 1× nonparticipating preference of 4,000; B has a senior 1× nonparticipating preference of 6,000. A explicitly consented to B's seniority at its financing. Both can optionally convert 1:1 to common and thereby relinquish their preference; there are no dividends or other adjustments. Each class chooses for itself, without side payments, to maximize its own cash given the other class's choice. Total available equity cash X is already net of all company debt and exit costs.

If both retain their preferences, B receives up to 6,000 first, A up to 4,000 next, and common gets what remains. If B retains but A converts, A shares the cash after B with common. Its fraction is 16/(64+16) = 20%, not 16%. Thus A's converted payment is 0.20(X−6,000) when X ≥ 6,000. It first matches its full preference at X = 26,000.

Once A converts, B compares keeping 6,000 with receiving 20% of total X after also converting. B's threshold is 30,000. When both convert above that point, A receives 0.16X ≥ 4,800 and will not revert to its 4,000 preference. Nor is “B converts, A retains” an omitted stable intermediate outcome: B would receive [20/(64+20)](X−4,000) and needs X ≥ 29,200 to match 6,000, whereas A would already prefer conversion whenever 0.16X > 4,000, that is X > 25,000. These conditions cannot both support A retaining and B converting. At low exits, retaining gives B all cash up to 6,000 and A the next cash up to 4,000; a unilateral conversion cannot improve either payment. At exact ties several choices can produce the same cash allocation.

Founders receive 42/64 of the common payment; the existing team receives 14/64 and the former pool's award holders 8/64. At X = 28,000, these payments are 11,550, 3,850 and 2,200. Adding all five groups gives exactly 28,000. The shortcut max(4,000, 0.16×28,000) would give A 4,480, which is wrong because B has retained its preference. The full cash pot and the actual remaining share count determine A's 4,400.

The waterfall is a payoff calculation, not a current fair-value estimate. To value a class, apply a consistent risk and timing valuation method to its payoffs across feasible outcomes, allowing for constraints and illiquidity where justified. Different claims on the same company cannot all be assigned the last preferred issue price merely because their conversion ratios are one. Conversely, an arbitrary “private-company discount” with no modeled rights or evidence does not repair a mistaken cap table.

6. Financing stages change choices and bargaining

Staged financing releases money after specified information or milestones rather than committing all usable cash at once. A technical validation, a repeat-customer target or a regulatory decision can make continuation more or less attractive. It can help investors stop an unproductive project, and successful learning can allow founders to negotiate later shares at a higher price. It also creates a financing deadline: a desirable project may be unable to continue if the next round is unavailable. Unless a binding commitment supplies the cash, a projected future round is a funding requirement, not a financing source already secured. The MIT lecture on control and staging provides the institutional motivation for separating these rights.

Specify who verifies the milestone, who decides continuation, the budget to reach it and the alternative if it fails. A sales target can be manipulated by discounting, while a technical target can be met without commercial demand. A contingent contract must account for these incentives. Contractual rights may include board appointments, class consent for major transactions, participation in later financing and rules for employee vesting. An economic ownership percentage does not, by itself, identify voting control or a veto. Staging and investor control can improve monitoring, but can also create costly renegotiation or conflict over sale timing.

An entrepreneur supplies capital, labor, time and concentrated exposure. Compare the venture with the best feasible alternative, including forgone wages, career development and personal liquidity needs. Separate the entrepreneur's employee wages from the value of the equity claim after those wages have been charged as a business cost. For example, suppose a founder's own risk assessment gives equity receipts a present certainty equivalent of 250, venture wages a present value of 20, and the required personal capital is 40. The venture package is 250+20−40 = 230. If the mutually exclusive employment alternative is worth 180 on the same personal basis, the incremental benefit is 50. These supplied certainty equivalents are not obtained by multiplying a preferred round price by common shares. Concentrated personal risk can make a diversified market discount rate inappropriate for that personal choice.

7. From portfolio proceeds to LP distributions

At the fund layer, specify commitments, actual calls, fee bases and payment dates, investments, distributions, retained cash and residual assets. Carried interest is the GP's contractually allocated share of specified profits. A distribution waterfall sets the order. A return-of-capital tier, a preferred-return hurdle, a GP catch-up, later profit sharing, recycling rights and a clawback can all change timing and amounts. A hurdle sets a qualifying LP return; a catch-up can direct subsequent proceeds toward a stated GP share; a clawback can require returning previously overpaid carry. None is silently present in our case.

Use one complete contract instead of applying a carry percentage to whichever “profit” looks largest. A whole-fund return-of-capital rule can defer carry until losses and expenses across the fund are covered. Paying carry early on individual successful deals requires explicit treatment of later losses and any clawback; simply adding separate deal profits can overstate final GP entitlement. Management fees can use different agreed bases over time, so a fee rate alone is insufficient.

Worked example 4 — Northpass's four dated ledgers

Northpass has an LP commitment of 200. It calls 100 at date 0, investing 90 and paying the manager a fee of 10. It calls 50 at date 1, investing 45 and paying a fee of 5. All fees count inside the commitment. There is no GP co-investment, fund borrowing, retained cash, recycling, other expense or tax. The portfolio pays the fund 60 at date 2 and 135 at date 3, after which all investments are liquidated and the remaining commitment is released.

The explicitly agreed waterfall first returns all LP contributions, including fee funding, then gives 20% of further proceeds to the GP as carry and 80% to LPs. There is no hurdle or catch-up. Because all contributions occur before distributions and carry is paid only at the final liquidation, no interim carry repayment is needed here.

Northpass cash reconciliation, kCU
ItemDate 0Date 1Date 2Date 3
LP calls1005000
Portfolio investments904500
Manager fees paid10500
Gross portfolio receipts0060135
LP capital returned006090
LP profit distributed00036
GP carry distributed0009
LP net cash flow−100−5060126

At date 2 the first 60 leaves unreturned capital of 90. At date 3, 135 first repays that 90; profit of 45 is split into 9 carry and 36 LP profit. The closing identities are: contributions 150 = investments 135 + fees 15; receipts 195 = LP distributions 186 + carry 9. Underlying investment profit 60 equals LP profit 36 + fees 15 + carry 9. Manager cash receipts are 24 before its own costs. Unused commitment of 50 is released; it is neither an investment loss nor an LP distribution.

The gross portfolio cash sequence is (−90, −45, 60, 135): MOIC = 195/135 = 1.4444444 and annual IRR = 16.8683%. The net LP sequence is (−100, −50, 60, 126): MOIC = 186/150 = 1.24 and annual IRR = 9.6112%. Those labels identify distinct cash-flow boundaries. In this case calls and investments coincide and there is no idle cash or borrowing; one must not presume such timing equivalence in another fund.

With annual dated cash Ct, an IRR solves Σ Ct/(1+r)t = 0, for r > −1. Northpass has two negative contributions rather than the single initial outlay in a conventional project. Uniqueness still follows because every contribution precedes every receipt. To see it, let k be the last contribution date and x = 1+r > 0. Accumulate earlier contributions to k and discount later receipts to k. The contribution magnitude is nondecreasing in x and bounded below by the positive last call; the receipt magnitude strictly decreases from infinity to zero. Their continuous difference crosses zero exactly once. A positive root requires total receipts to exceed total contributions. With interleaved calls and distributions this argument no longer applies; there can be multiple roots or none, and dated cash plus benchmark NPV must be examined.

For irregular calendar dates, use the actual timing under a stated year-fraction convention rather than pretending every receipt is annual. MOIC ignores holding time; IRR is sensitive to timing and scale. Neither ranks mutually exclusive investments reliably without comparable risk, capital requirements and opportunity costs.

8. Separate marks, timing effects and evidence of skill

For LP reporting, define DPI as cumulative distributions divided by paid-in capital, RVPI as residual LP net asset value divided by paid-in capital, and TVPI = DPI+RVPI. Paid-in capital here includes contributions for every purpose. A gross investment multiple instead uses investment capital, as explicitly labeled. The ILPA performance definitions distinguish portfolio and fund cash flows, investor net returns, marks and subscription-facility effects; these distinctions motivate our reporting boundaries, not an assertion that every fund has Northpass's terms.

Suppose immediately after Northpass's date-2 distribution, the remaining portfolio has a 100 mark expressed as estimated net sale cash if liquidated then. For this interim example, allocate that hypothetical liquidation through the same waterfall. Unreturned LP capital is 90, so estimated carry is 0.20(100−90) = 2 and LP residual NAV is 98. The ratios are DPI = 60/150 = 0.40, RVPI = 98/150 = 0.6533333, TVPI = 158/150 = 1.0533333. The 2 is an accrual under the stipulated liquidation-mark convention, not carry already paid or a universal fair-value rule. The 98 is not cash received. At final liquidation, RVPI is zero and DPI = TVPI = 1.24.

A subscription facility is fund borrowing supported by specified capital commitments. Its interest and repayment remain fund obligations. Consider a separate investment costing 100 at date 0 and realizing 144 at date 2, with no fee or carry. Direct LP funding at date 0 gives MOIC 1.44 and two-year annual IRR 20%. Alternatively, a stipulated line advances 100 at date 0, charges 8% for one year and is fully repaid with an LP call of 108 at date 1. The LP receives 144 at date 2. Its MOIC falls to 144/108 = 1⅓, while its one-year IRR rises to 33⅓%. The investment itself still earns 20%; 8 has been spent on funding. Delaying a capital call changes the reported LP timing and the fund's obligations. This is not improved operating performance. Capacity to meet the 108 call was committed before it arrived.

A credible performance comparison therefore records the cash-flow boundary, dates, currencies, investment strategy, leverage, fees and carry, fund size, realized proceeds and residual valuation policy. Compare vintages—cohorts formed or first investing under a stated date definition—because entry markets, financing conditions, holding periods and available exits differ. A sample selected only from realized exits can omit long-held failures or unresolved successes. Voluntary reporting, missing funds and exclusion of managers that never raise another fund can change apparent averages or persistence. State the inclusion rule and examine the omitted population rather than assuming any database covers it.

Kaplan and Strömberg explicitly discuss realized-exit selection, incomplete fund samples and cohort comparisons in their historical review. That supports the need for sample scrutiny, not a current numerical claim about private-market returns. Matching public benchmarks by cash timing helps comparison, but remaining differences in risk, leverage, liquidity and access still matter. A successful selected deal, a large marked-up position or a high net IRR does not by itself establish a manager's causal contribution, general outperformance or an attainable return for every prospective LP.

9. Reproduce the claims before defending a decision

The lab guide, fictional inputs, standard-library Python model and reference output run offline. Rational arithmetic closes the budgets, share counts and waterfalls; only numerical IRRs use floating-point root solving. Copy the three program/input/output files to one directory and run python3 v08-c10-analysis.py to compare results. The guide identifies supported variations and failure reports.

First reconcile Mistral's acquisition and all annual cash. Then change first-year EBITDA to 50: a reported financing failure is the intended result until a dated, authorized top-up is provided. Next compare Saffron's cash allocations just below and above each conversion threshold, testing each class's alternative action while holding the other's action fixed. Finally reconcile Northpass's portfolio, fee, LP and carry ledgers. The review checker separately reconstructs the displayed results and all eight exercise anchors; passing arithmetic does not establish actual investment feasibility, an empirical causal effect or legal enforceability.

10. Exercises

  1. Entry price and attribution. Mistral's entry EV rises to 390 with entry EBITDA still 60. Every other original base-case input, including debt of 210, fees, operating forecasts and exit multiple, stays fixed. Rebuild seller proceeds and sources/uses, calculate sponsor MOIC and IRR, and reconcile sponsor cash gain using the stated earnings-then-multiple decomposition. Explain why the unchanged exit price does not preserve the original return.
  2. A cash shortfall needs money. Mistral's year-1 EBITDA is 50; all other operating inputs remain as in the original case. Calculate cash tax, available principal cash and the financing gap without new support. Then assume an explicitly authorized sponsor contribution equal to that gap at date 1, all applied to debt service. Restore original EBITDA in years 2 and 3. Compute closing debt each year, exit equity, the complete sponsor cash sequence, MOIC and IRR. Explain why placing all contributions at date 0 would be wrong.
  3. A different option pool. A new fictional venture has 4,000 thousand founder and 1,000 thousand team common shares. It raises 3,000 at pre-money 12,000, with a new pre-round pool equal to 15% of the post-round fully diluted shares. There are no other claims. Calculate pool shares, price, investor shares and all four final fractions. Explain why a founder cannot infer personal wealth merely from its fraction of headline post-money.
  4. A down round. Return to Saffron's original post-A shares, but set B pre-money to 12,000 and its primary cash to 6,000. Keep all conversion ratios unchanged and add no pool, fee or anti-dilution protection. Calculate the price, B shares, total shares and all five ownership fractions. Compare founders' dilution with the original B round and identify the cash destination.
  5. Joint preferred choices. Use the original post-B Saffron cap table and original preferred contract, not the down-round variant. Allocate exits of 9,000, 27,000 and 40,000 to B, A and common. Show the conversion comparisons determining the two high-exit thresholds and why B converting alone is not a missing stable regime. At 27,000, calculate founders' payment and identify the error in using max(4,000, 0.16X) for A.
  6. Participation is a different contract. A separate venture has only common and one preferred class. The preferred investment/preference is 4,000, its as-converted common fraction is 25%, and there are no dividends or other claims. Compare preferred and common payments at total equity exits of 2,000, 12,000, 24,000 and 40,000 for three contracts: 1× nonparticipating with conversion; 1× uncapped participating; and participation capped at twice the preference with optional common conversion retained. Derive the nonparticipating conversion threshold and the cap's two upper breakpoints.
  7. A weaker final fund exit. Northpass's final gross receipt is 105 instead of 135. All calls, fees, earlier receipts and carry terms are unchanged, and all assets are liquidated at date 3. Rebuild the final capital/profit/carry distribution, compute gross portfolio and net LP MOIC and IRR, and state final DPI, RVPI and TVPI. Reconcile the underlying cash gain among LP profit, fees and carry.
  8. Timing versus skill. Reconstruct both financing routes for the 100 investment with 144 receipt at date 2 from Section 8, including the line's date-0 advance and date-1 repayment. Prove the underlying investment return is unchanged despite different LP IRRs and MOICs. An analyst uses the higher LP IRR to claim superior skill and recommends comparing only exited deals from surviving managers. Evaluate both claims and name at least four additional comparison requirements.
Complete solutions and evaluation criteria

  1. Seller equity proceeds become 390+20−80 = 330. Uses are 330+80+10+4 = 424; sources are debt 210, acquired cash 20 and sponsor 194. The debt and operating schedules do not change, so exit equity remains 275.76184. MOIC = 275.76184/194 = 1.4214528; IRR = (275.76184/194)1/3−1 = 12.4374%.

    Entry multiple is 390/60 = 6.5. Earnings growth contributes 6.5(72−60) = 78; multiple change contributes (6−6.5)72 = −36; debt reduction contributes 61.76184; fees remove 22. Their sum is 81.76184, exactly 275.76184−194. Paying an additional 30 at entry with the same future receipt reduces gain by 30 and lowers both return measures. A complete answer keeps the price change out of the fixed operating/debt inputs.

  2. Interest is 16.8; tax is 0.25(50−12−16.8) = 5.3. Available principal cash is 50−5.3−16.8−16−3 = 8.9, against required principal 15. The unfinanced gap is 6.1; without authorized support the plan is infeasible and an ordinary successful-exit IRR would misrepresent it.

    The sponsor contributes 6.1 at date 1, allowing principal repayment of 15 and closing debt of 195. Year 2 has interest 15.6, tax 10.1 and sweep 20.3, leaving 174.7. Year 3 has interest 13.976, tax 11.506 and sweep 21.518, leaving 153.182. Exit equity is 432−8−153.182 = 270.818. The sponsor sequence is (−164, −6.1, 0, 270.818). Total contributions are 170.1, MOIC is 1.5921105, and the root of −164−6.1/(1+r)+270.818/(1+r)3 = 0 is 16.9714%. Dating the entire 170.1 at zero would give the later contribution a fictitious extra holding year. Net cash gain is 100.718; equivalently 72+56.818−22−6.1 = 100.718. The extra contribution is counted in financing and investor return exactly once.

  3. Here a = 3,000/12,000 = 1/4 and h = 3/20, so P = (3/16)(5,000+P). Therefore P = 15,000/13 thousand shares. Pre-round fully diluted shares are 80,000/13, price is 12,000/(80,000/13) = 1.95 CU, investor shares are 20,000/13 thousand and post-round total is 100,000/13 thousand. Fractions are founders 52%, team 13%, pool 15% and investor 20%.

    Credit the explanation for identifying the exact pricing denominator, the reserve's unissued status and at least one reason why headline common wealth does not follow: distinct preferred rights, uncertainty and timing of exit, or personal concentration/illiquidity and opportunity costs. The arithmetic 52%×15,000 = 7,800 is a headline multiplication, not an independently established common-share fair value or spendable wealth.

  4. The original post-A total is 80,000/7 thousand. B's price is 12,000/(80,000/7) = 1.05 CU, new shares are 40,000/7 thousand and final total is 120,000/7 thousand. Fractions are founders 35%, team 7/60 = 11⅔%, pool 1/15 = 6⅔%, A 2/15 = 13⅓%, and B 1/3 = 33⅓%. They sum to one. Earlier fractions are multiplied by 2/3, versus 0.8 in the original B round. Founder shares stay at 6,000, but their percentage falls to 35% instead of 42%. All 6,000 goes to the company, not the founders or A. No protection is invented for A; such a protection would require recalculating the conversion counts under specified terms.

  5. At 9,000, B gets 6,000, A 3,000 and common zero. At 27,000, B keeps 6,000, A converts for 0.2(27,000−6,000) = 4,200, and common receives 16,800. Founders receive (42/64)16,800 = 11,025. At 40,000, both convert: B 8,000, A 6,400, common 25,600.

    With B retaining, A's conversion threshold solves 0.2(X−6,000) = 4,000, giving 26,000. With A converting, B's threshold solves 0.2X = 6,000, giving 30,000. B converting while A retains requires [20/84](X−4,000) ≥ 6,000, or X ≥ 29,200. But given B converted, A prefers conversion when 0.16X > 4,000, or X > 25,000. Thus the alleged B-only regime cannot be mutually optimal. The naive A formula at 27,000 gives 4,320; the true converted residual excludes B's 6,000 and uses an 80% remaining share denominator, producing 4,200. Full credit requires both the priority and denominator reasoning, not just the table.

  6. Preferred/common payments under the three contracts, kCU
    Exit XNonparticipatingUncapped participatingCapped plus conversion
    2,0002,000 / 02,000 / 02,000 / 0
    12,0004,000 / 8,0006,000 / 6,0006,000 / 6,000
    24,0006,000 / 18,0009,000 / 15,0008,000 / 16,000
    40,00010,000 / 30,00013,000 / 27,00010,000 / 30,000

    Nonparticipating conversion matches the full preference at 0.25X = 4,000, so X = 16,000. Participating proceeds above X = 4,000 are 4,000+0.25(X−4,000). They reach the cap 8,000 at X = 20,000. Capped proceeds remain 8,000 until conversion reaches that amount at X = 32,000, after which conversion is better. At low exits no preference creates money beyond X. At high exits retaining the capped participation and also taking conversion would count incompatible alternatives twice.

  7. After date-2 distribution of 60, unreturned LP capital remains 90. Final receipt of 105 returns 90, leaving profit 15; carry is 3, LP profit 12, and final LP distribution 102. Gross portfolio flows are (−90, −45, 60, 105), MOIC 165/135 = 1.2222222, IRR 9.1066%. Net LP flows are (−100, −50, 60, 102), MOIC 162/150 = 1.08, IRR 3.4086%. Final DPI = TVPI = 1.08 and RVPI = 0.

    Underlying investment gain is 165−135 = 30, allocated to LP profit 12, fees 15 and carry 3. Carry is not 20% of 30 because this contract returns all 150 of LP contributions before charging it; investment-only capital of 135 is not the agreed return-of-capital base. The unused commitment remains 50.

  8. Direct route: LP contributes 100 at date 0; the fund invests it then, receives 144 at date 2 and distributes 144. LP flows are (−100, 0, 144), MOIC 1.44, annual IRR 20%. Line route: lender advances 100 at date 0 and the fund invests 100; the LP contributes 108 at date 1 and the fund pays the lender principal 100 plus interest 8; at date 2 it receives and distributes 144. LP flows are (0, −108, 144), MOIC 4/3, IRR 1/3. Lender flows (−100, 108) earn the stipulated 8%. In both routes the operating investment has flows (−100, 0, 144) and annual return 20%. The LP's shorter funded duration raises its IRR despite a lower multiple and an 8 financing cost. Future call obligations and their liquidity cost do not disappear before the call date.

    Evaluate the critique for: (i) separating operating performance from financing timing and avoiding a skill claim based on IRR alone; (ii) identifying that exited-only and surviving-manager samples can exclude relevant unfavorable and unresolved outcomes; and (iii) naming at least four relevant comparison controls, such as full dated cash flows, fee/carry treatment, portfolio versus fund boundary, subscription and company leverage, vintage, strategy/risk, currency, realized versus marked value, inclusion of failed/unreported funds, investment scale or investor access. Other well-explained requirements earn equal credit. Neither “all private funds outperform” nor “all private funds underperform” follows from this evidence.

Teach-back and delayed retention

Teach-back. Explain to a founder why a 42% fully diluted stake is not a promise to receive 42% of every exit, and to an LP why a sponsor's deal IRR is not the LP's return. Answer standard: distinguish the capitalization count from contractual preferred priority and actual conversion choices; use Saffron's 18,000 exit, where founders receive 5,250 rather than 7,560. Then identify calls, fees, carry and dates at the fund boundary; Northpass's 16.8683% gross portfolio IRR becomes 9.6112% net to LPs. A successful explanation closes each cash pot without implying these terms apply to every deal.

Delayed check. Without the tables: (a) Why does Mistral require 164 of sponsor equity rather than 144? (b) When B retains 6,000, what fraction of Saffron's remaining equity cash does converted A receive? (c) At Northpass's date-2 mark of 100, what are net LP NAV and TVPI? (d) Does deferring a capital call prove a better investment? Answers: (a) Entry sponsor cash is 360−210+14 = 164; the acquired excess cash of 20 was already included in seller equity and then used once as a source, so deducting it again produces 144 incorrectly. (b) 16/(64+16) = 20%; the B preference is paid before allocating that residual. (c) Unreturned capital is 90, hypothetical carry accrual is 2, LP NAV is 98, and TVPI is (60+98)/150 = 1.0533333. (d) No: the same 100-to-144 investment keeps its 20% underlying IRR while borrowing changes costs, obligations and LP cash timing.

Sources and extension

The inspected sources are Kaplan and Strömberg, Leveraged Buyouts and Private Equity, author-hosted prepublication version; Antoinette Schoar's MIT lectures on venture contracts, preferred payoffs and implied valuations and control, employee terms and staged financing; and ILPA's 2025 performance-template definitions. The source record identifies inspected sections and version limits. Historical descriptions and empirical sample findings are not current legal requirements, current market terms or investment forecasts. All numerical contracts, cases, derivations and exercises here were constructed for this chapter.

Deeper work should value contingent claims under coherent risk assumptions, model uncertainty and financing feasibility across operating paths, read actual governing documents, and study fund performance with transparent inclusion rules and dated cash flows. Our two-class conversion proof does not establish a general algorithm for every capital structure. The next distress and restructuring chapter develops what happens when a company's assets and obligations cannot be reconciled by the promised payments; it should not be replaced by an unexplained refinancing assumption.

Sources and further study

  • Steven N. Kaplan and Per Strömberg — Leveraged Buyouts and Private Equity (author-hosted prepublication version) — Historical institutional background: separation of buyout firms, funds and portfolio companies; commitments, fees and carry; exit routes; realized-exit selection, cohort timing and incomplete fund samples. No historical performance estimate, current term prevalence or causal outperformance claim is imported.
  • Antoinette Schoar, MIT 15.431 Spring 2011 — Venture Capital Contracts: Part I — Specialist background for contractual preferred versus common payoffs, optional conversion, participation and the limitation of headline pre/post-money valuations. The two-round pool algebra, two-class joint conversion proof and every chapter input are original.
  • Antoinette Schoar, MIT 15.431 Spring 2011 — Venture Capital Contracts: Part II — Background for separate control rights, milestones, employee reserved shares, staged financing and conditional future funding. Original chapter cap tables expressly exclude anti-dilution adjustments and specify actual award issuance at exit.
  • ILPA Performance Template Definitions — Granular Methodology, v1.1 (2025 PDF) — Reporting-boundary reference: fee and investment calls, commitments, carry/clawback, subscription facilities, investor net versus portfolio gross cash flows, residual NAV and net TVPI. Northpass's simplified waterfall is an original stipulated contract, not represented as an ILPA requirement or full template implementation.
